This activity demonstrates how to determine the orthogonal projection of a vector onto a subspace of $\real^m$.

Let's begin by considering a line $L$, defined by the vector $\wvec=\twovec21$, and a vector $\bvec=\twovec24$ not on $L$, as illustrated in [fig-projection-line-c].

Finding the orthogonal projection of $\bvec$ onto the line defined by $\wvec$.

To find $\bhat$, first notice that $\bhat = s\wvec$ for some scalar $s$. Since $\bvec-\bhat = \bvec - s\wvec$ is orthogonal to $\wvec$, what do we know about the dot product $$ (\bvec-s\wvec)\cdot\wvec\text{?} $$

Apply the distributive property of dot products to find the scalar $s$. What is the vector $\bhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\bvec$ onto $L$?

More generally, explain why the orthogonal projection of $\bvec$ onto the line defined by $\wvec$ is $$ \bhat= \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec}{\wvec\cdot\wvec}~\wvec\text{.} $$

The same ideas apply more generally. Suppose we have an orthogonal set of vectors $\wvec_1=\threevec22{-1}$ and $\wvec_2=\threevec102$ that define a plane $W$ in $\real^3$. If $\bvec=\threevec396$ another vector in $\real^3$, we seek the vector $\bhat$ on the plane $W$ closest to $\bvec$. As before, the vector $\bvec-\bhat$ will be orthogonal to $W$, as illustrated in [fig-3d-orthog].

Given a plane $W$ defined by the orthogonal vectors $\wvec_1$ and $\wvec_2$ and another vector $\bvec$, we seek the vector $\bhat$ on $W$ closest to $\bvec$.

The vector $\bvec-\bhat$ is orthogonal to $W$. What does this say about the dot products: $(\bvec-\bhat)\cdot\wvec_1$ and $(\bvec-\bhat)\cdot\wvec_2$?

Since $\bhat$ is in the plane $W$, we can write it as a linear combination $\bhat = c_1\wvec_1 + c_2\wvec_2$. Then $$ \bvec-\bhat = \bvec - (c_1\wvec_1+c_2\wvec_2)\text{.} $$ Find the weight $c_1$ by dotting $\bvec-\bhat$ with $\wvec_1$ and applying the distributive property of dot products. Similarly, find the weight $c_2$.

What is the vector $\bhat$, the orthogonal projection of $\bvec$ onto the plane $W$?

Suppose that $W$ is a subspace of $\real^m$ with orthogonal basis $\wvec_1,\wvec_2,\ldots,\wvec_n$ and that $\bvec$ is a vector in $\real^m$. Explain why the orthogonal projection of $\bvec$ onto $W$ is the vector $$ \bhat = \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec_1}{\wvec_1\cdot\wvec_1}~\wvec_1 + \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec_2}{\wvec_2\cdot\wvec_2}~\wvec_2 + \cdots + \frac{\bvec\cdot\wvec_n}{\wvec_n\cdot\wvec_n}~\wvec_n\text{.} $$

Suppose that $\uvec_1,\uvec_2,\ldots,\uvec_n$ is an orthonormal basis for $W$; that is, the vectors are orthogonal to one another and have unit length. Explain why the orthogonal projection is $$ \bhat= (\bvec\cdot\uvec_1)~\uvec_1 + (\bvec\cdot\uvec_2)~\uvec_2 + \cdots + (\bvec\cdot\uvec_n)~\uvec_n\text{.} $$

If $Q=\begin{bmatrix} \uvec_1 \amp \uvec_2 \amp \ldots \amp \uvec_n \end{bmatrix} $ is the matrix whose columns are an orthonormal basis of $W$, use [prop-transpose-multiplication] to explain why $\bhat = QQ^T\bvec$.
